artworkData.intro: Vigée Le Brun’s pared-down portrait of a wigless Hubert Robert presents him as a natural and enlightened figure, fitting characteristics for the period’s leading landscape painter. Although created as an unusual pendant to a self-portrait by Vigée Le Brun, the painting’s story extends beyond artistic friendship. Its journey through collections of elite patrons reveals the colonial wealth that underpinned Paris’s art world, and traces how those networks of money, art, and influence continued to shape France’s cultural institutions long after the French and Haitian Revolutions.

provenanceEvents.title: 1. Artists, Networks, and Colonial Wealth in 1780s Paris
provenanceEvents.text:
Vigée Lebrun’s portrait of Hubert Robert made its debut at the Paris Salon of 1789, the biennial showcase of the Academy’s latest works. It can be glimpsed on the wall in Wailly’s drawing depicting the spectacle of this exhibition at the Louvre. Both sitter and painter were stars of the Paris art world in the 1780s: Robert’s landscapes and Vigée Lebrun’s portraits were sought-after commodities for the city’s elites.

This portrait of Robert was conceived a year or two before the exhibition, painted as a pendant to Vigée Le Brun’s self-portrait with her daughter Julie, exhibited at the previous Salon of 1787. Such a pairing was extremely unusual for a man and woman who were neither married nor related. Together, the portraits made a striking statement about artistic identity, celebrity, and professional affiliation. Rather than proclaiming a romantic relationship between these artists, they presented Vigée Le Brun as Robert’s colleague: a leading artist, a fellow academician, and participant in the same social and professional networks.

Those networks extended through her husband, the art dealer Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Le Brun, to a wide circle of patrons and collectors, including many whose fortunes derived from colonial trade and enslavement. Among them was the banker, slave trader, and planter Jean-Joseph de Laborde, who acquired both these artists’ portraits. The exact date of purchase is unknown, but Laborde almost certainly already owned them when Robert’s portrait appeared in the Salon of 1789, just weeks after the storming of the Bastille marked the beginning of the French Revolution.

provenanceEvents.title: 2. Painter and Patron: Robert and Laborde
provenanceEvents.text:
By the time Laborde acquired Robert’s portrait on the eve of the Revolution, the two had established a close creative and financial relationship as artist and patron. That relationship connected Robert directly to the wealth generated by France’s colonial economy.

Laborde had become one of the richest men in France by the 1780s, amassing his fortune through banking and transatlantic trade. He trafficked enslaved Africans to the Caribbean, imported colonial products into France, and owned a large swathe of interconnected sugar plantations in Saint-Domingue. Robert, too, had family connections to Saint-Domingue – his brother was sent there in a military capacity by the duc de Choiseul and lived there for several years. This placed both artist and patron within networks shaped by the colony’s profitable and brutal plantation system.

In 1784, Laborde used some of his fortune to purchase and lavishly renovate his grand country estate, the Château de Méréville. Robert was commissioned to design its extensive park and gardens, as well as to paint landscapes for the château’s interior and numerous views of the Méréville grounds. Laborde kept most of these Méréville views in his Paris residence, where he also displayed his pendant portraits of Robert and Vigée Le Brun.

In this way, Laborde’s colonial wealth helped finance both Robert and Vigée Le Brun’s artistic work, supporting the creation of the landscapes and portraits for which they were celebrated.

provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Hubert Robert, View of the Park of Méréville, c. 1790.

provenanceEvents.title: 3. Revolutionary Confiscation, Return, and Colonial Family Legacies
provenanceEvents.text:
In 1793, the portrait of Robert was seized from Laborde’s Paris residence on the rue d’Artois along with the rest of his art collection. As the French Revolution intensified, the revolutionary state confiscated the property of suspected enemies of the new regime, like Laborde, who was arrested and later executed by guillotine in 1794.

Many artworks confiscated during the Revolution became founding objects in the Louvre’s collection when it was opened as a public museum in 1793 as part of the revolutionary project. But although Robert’s portrait would end up there, that was not its trajectory.

Instead, this portrait and many other artworks were returned to the Laborde family in Year IX (c. 1801). The details are not precisely known, but it was probably returned to Laborde’s widow, Rosalie de Nettine, or possibly to their eldest surviving son, Alexandre de Laborde.

Sometime thereafter, the portrait of Robert passed into the collection of Laborde’s only daughter, Nathalie de Laborde. She was granted the painting in usufruct, a legal arrangement allowing her to possess this item of family property during her lifetime without actually owning it.

The portrait’s passage through the Laborde family shows how the French and Haitian Revolutions of the 1790s did not necessarily disrupt pre-existing systems of colonial wealth. Those financial legacies instead carried through to subsequent generations.
provenanceEvents.imageSource: Augustin Pajou, Bust of Nathalie de Laborde, 1789. @GrandPalaisRmn (musée du Louvre) / René-Gabriel Ojéda.
provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Augustin Pajou, Bust of Nathalie de Laborde, 1789.

provenanceEvents.title: 4. Back to the Artist: Vigée Le Brun and the Louvre
provenanceEvents.text:
When Nathalie de Laborde died in 1835, Robert’s portrait did not stay with the Laborde family. Instead, it was ‘returned’ once again – this time to the artist who painted it.

Vigée Le Brun was then 80 years old. She had been about 30 when she painted the portrait. Despite her royal and aristocratic connections, she had survived the French Revolution by fleeing Paris in 1789 and spending over a decade as an émigré, painting portraits of elites across Europe. Her husband, meanwhile, remained in Paris. Le Brun had been the principal art dealer to many of Paris’s elite colonial collectors, including Laborde, but he successfully distanced himself from these associations and went on to work officially for the new regime’s arts administration. This included shaping the new Louvre museum by determining which confiscated artworks would enter the collection.

Decades later, Vigée Le Brun’s will revealed her own intentions for the Louvre. She wanted three paintings in her possession to enter the collection, of which two were the pendant portraits of Robert and herself with Julie. When she died in 1842, she bequeathed the works to her niece, Eugénie Tripier Le Franc, with instructions that she donate them to the museum. She did so, and both portraits entered the Louvre in 1843.
